after: ## How do traditional and new media differ?
alt: Left: a single broadcaster sends content one-way to many audience members. Right: a network of users all connected to each other. Below, traditional media are one-to-many, gatekept, scheduled, national and costly to enter; new media are many-to-many, user-generated, on demand, global and cheap to enter.
caption: Traditional media broadcast from one to many; new media connect many to many.

after: ## Who controls the media? The main theories
alt: A grid compares pluralism, instrumental Marxism, neo-Marxism and postmodernism on who controls the media, how control works and key sociologists. Pluralists say audiences, instrumental Marxists say owners, neo-Marxists say hegemonic ruling-class ideas, and postmodernists say no single source.
caption: Theories disagree on whether audiences, owners, shared ideas or no one controls the media.

after: ## Who controls the media? The main theories
alt: A funnel in which all possible stories pass through five filters: ownership, advertising, reliance on official sources, flak and anti-communism, leaving the news that is published.
caption: Five filters narrow all possible stories down to the news that fits elite interests.

after: ## Who controls the media? The main theories
alt: Top chain: in the manipulation model owners give orders, journalists comply and ruling-class ideology is spread. Bottom chain: in the hegemonic model mostly middle-class journalists share a common-sense view, so ruling-class ideas dominate without orders.
caption: Manipulation is deliberate control by owners; hegemony works through shared assumptions.

after: ## What influences the selection and presentation of news?
alt: Seven influences surround the question of what becomes news: news values, gatekeeping, commercial pressures, owners, sources, practical constraints and censorship.
caption: News is selected, not simply reported: seven pressures shape what appears.

after: ## How might the media influence the political process?
alt: Agenda setting: when the media emphasise issues, voters rate those issues as most important, so the media tell people what to think about. Opinion polls, news reporting and social media are three further routes of influence.
caption: The media shape which issues voters think about, as well as how they see them.
